paragraphs: Fairness objectives often describe how to distribute wellbeing across groups, while machine learning systems commonly minimize prediction losses. Connecting these perspectives requires deciding how losses translate into utility. This paper develops a complementary framework that works directly with group harms, avoiding the need to first construct utility functions for a welfare objective.

The authors introduce malfare, a measure that combines groups’ expected losses into an assessment of societal harm. They justify it using the standard axioms of cardinal welfare. A central theoretical finding is that minimizing malfare is not equivalent to simply treating negative loss as utility and maximizing welfare: the axioms distinguish these constructions.

The paper then defines fair-PAC learning, which requires learning a model close to optimal malfare with controlled error probability and bounded sample requirements. Under identified conditions, standard PAC learners can become fair-PAC learners. These conversions provide statistical efficiency guarantees, and computational efficiency in some cases, connecting the axiomatic framework to concrete training algorithms with generalization guarantees.
neurips-2021-an-axiomatic-theory-of-prov.tldr: The paper formalizes fairness through group-level harm minimization and establishes conditions for learning near-optimal models with statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Neural models based on differential equations must solve a dynamical system to produce their outputs. This paper introduces Multiple Shooting Layers, an implicit neural model that approaches this computation through methods designed to work across time in parallel. The goal is to make differential-equation-based inference more efficient while retaining its role within trainable neural architectures.

The layers solve initial value problems using parallelizable root-finding algorithms. This makes the numerical solution method a central part of the model design. The authors develop a framework for these layers and examine alternative solution methods from both theoretical and computational perspectives, connecting algorithmic choices to the work required for inference.

Multiple Shooting Layers are presented as broadly usable replacements for Neural ODEs, with improvements in function evaluations and elapsed inference time. Demonstrations cover long-horizon control involving ordinary and partial differential equations, plus latent models for sequence generation. The paper also investigates inference speedups in Neural CDEs used to classify medical time series, extending the approach across several kinds of dynamical learning tasks.
neurips-2021-differentiable-multiple-sho.tldr: Multiple Shooting Layers use parallelizable differential-equation solvers to improve the inference efficiency of neural dynamical models.

paragraphs: DROID-SLAM tackles the linked problems of estimating a camera’s pose and recovering scene depth from video. Its deep learning system repeatedly updates both quantities, rather than producing a single set of estimates. Camera pose describes the camera’s position and orientation, while pixelwise depth gives a detailed representation of the scene visible in each image.

The central component is a Dense Bundle Adjustment layer that participates in these recurrent updates. This places joint refinement of pose and depth inside the system’s iterative computation. The approach matters because the output is both a description of camera motion and a spatial interpretation of the images, with the two estimates updated together.

The authors report large accuracy improvements over prior work and substantially fewer catastrophic failures. They also show flexibility across camera inputs: although trained using monocular video, DROID-SLAM can use stereo or RGB-D video at test time for improved performance. That finding indicates that its learned system can benefit from additional visual or depth information without requiring those input formats during training.
neurips-2021-droid-slam-deep-visual-slam.tldr: DROID-SLAM repeatedly refines camera pose and dense depth, reporting improved accuracy and robustness across several camera formats.

paragraphs: Learning to detect a new object category from very few examples can produce poorly organized internal representations. The paper argues that conventional fine-tuning may implicitly borrow from several previously learned categories, scattering the new category’s features and making classes harder to distinguish. FADI addresses this through two explicit stages of knowledge transfer and separation.

First, the association stage matches each new category to a familiar category using semantic similarity. The new category then imitates that particular category’s established feature space, encouraging a compact representation. This gives the transfer process a specific reference instead of allowing the new representation to draw implicitly from multiple base categories.

Next, the discrimination stage separates classification branches for base and novel categories so that imitation does not leave the paired classes indistinguishable. A specialized margin loss further encourages separation across classes. Experiments on Pascal VOC and MS-COCO report state-of-the-art performance and substantial baseline improvements. The advantage is especially pronounced when only one or three examples are available, supporting the usefulness of organizing transfer carefully under severe data scarcity.
neurips-2021-few-shot-object-detection-v.tldr: FADI improves few-shot detection by first associating novel categories with familiar ones and then explicitly separating their representations.

paragraphs: A summarization model needs a search procedure to turn its predictions into a complete summary. This paper targets the local optimality problem in ordinary beam search: decisions made while building a summary may not align well with a desirable complete result. Its proposed search method uses a global view of attention to guide those decisions.

The authors define a protocol describing how a globally optimal candidate should distribute attention over the source. They then build a scoring mechanism that uses this distribution to regulate beam search at each step. Crucially, the global attention distribution can be predicted before inference, making the overall guidance available while individual summary choices are still being made.

The intended result is generation closer to a global optimum under this attention-based framework. Across nine datasets, the method significantly improves state-of-the-art summarization models, including when using empirical hyperparameters. It also continues to produce meaningful text when attention distributions are corrupted. These findings support both the usefulness of global guidance and resilience to imperfect attention information, without establishing universally optimal summaries.
neurips-2021-global-aware-beam-search-fo.tldr: Global-aware beam search guides summary generation with a predicted overall attention distribution, improving summarization across nine datasets.

paragraphs: A stochastic process describes a random trajectory, but its complete path does not by itself capture how information becomes available over time. That evolving information is its filtration. This paper develops representations that account for this distinction, which matters when a task depends on what can be known at a particular moment.

The authors condition processes on their filtrations to construct higher-order kernel mean embeddings. From these representations, they derive higher-order maximum mean discrepancies and empirical estimators with consistency guarantees. A resulting two-sample test can detect filtration-related information that a standard MMD test misses, extending what kernel-based comparisons can distinguish between stochastic processes.

The framework also yields universal kernels for regression on stochastic processes. The authors use these for financial calibration and optimal stopping problems, including American option pricing, where the timing of information is relevant to decisions. Finally, they adapt conditional independence tests to processes and develop a causal-discovery algorithm for recovering structural dependencies among interacting bodies from observed multidimensional trajectories.
neurips-2021-higher-order-kernel-mean-em.tldr: Higher-order kernel embeddings capture how information unfolds in stochastic processes, supporting richer statistical tests, regression, and causal discovery.

paragraphs: Zero-shot recognition transfers knowledge from familiar categories to categories without training examples by connecting visual features with semantic information. HSVA addresses a weakness in learning that connection: aligning overall distributions alone may leave the internal structures of the two representations mismatched. The paper therefore separates alignment into structure adaptation and distribution adaptation.

For structure adaptation, two task-specific encoders map visual and semantic data into a common space. A supervised adversarial discrepancy module reduces disagreement between two classifiers’ predictions, encouraging closer alignment of the feature structures. The subsequent distribution stage uses a common encoder and minimizes Wasserstein distance between latent multivariate Gaussian distributions.

Both stages are combined within a framework built from two partially aligned variational autoencoders. This provides a coordinated way to address two different sources of mismatch instead of expecting a single adaptation step to resolve both. Experiments on four benchmark datasets report superior performance in conventional and generalized zero-shot learning. The findings support the proposed hierarchy across both evaluated recognition settings.
neurips-2021-hsva-hierarchical-semantic-.tldr: HSVA improves zero-shot recognition by aligning the structures and then the distributions of visual and semantic representations.

paragraphs: Sparse linear bandits model repeated decisions in high-dimensional settings where the underlying reward structure is sparse. Each choice has two consequences: it earns a reward and reveals information that may improve later decisions. This paper studies information-directed sampling as a way to balance the value of learning against the regret incurred while exploring.

The authors develop information-theoretic bounds on Bayesian regret. These bounds nearly match existing lower bounds across a variety of problem instances, providing evidence that the method adapts to different information and reward structures. The result concerns the cumulative cost of decisions under the Bayesian formulation, connecting exploration choices to formal performance guarantees.

For practical implementation, the paper proposes empirical Bayesian posterior sampling with a spike-and-slab Gaussian-Laplace prior. This supplies a sparsity-oriented mechanism for representing uncertainty within the sampling procedure. Numerical experiments report significant regret reductions relative to several baselines. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support information-directed exploration as an effective approach for the sparse linear bandit problems considered.
neurips-2021-information-directed-sampli.tldr: Sparse information-directed sampling combines adaptive regret guarantees with a practical Bayesian implementation that reduces regret in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Unsupervised object discovery seeks objects in images without object annotations. Existing approaches face a scaling problem: handling large collections can require approximations that hurt performance. This paper reformulates discovery as a ranking task, allowing it to draw on distributed techniques for eigenvalue problems and link analysis rather than relying on those compromises.

The resulting Large-scale Object Discovery approach, or LOD, also uses self-supervised features to form a fully unsupervised pipeline. This addresses the source of the image representation as well as the discovery procedure itself. The authors evaluate both finding one prominent object per image and finding multiple objects within each image.

On COCO and OpenImages, single-object results match or exceed prior state of the art at medium scale, up to 120,000 images. At 1.7 million images, the reported improvement exceeds 37% over the other scalable algorithms. For multiple-object discovery, average precision improves by over 14% across datasets from 20,000 to 1.7 million images. Self-supervised features also yield state-of-the-art discovery performance on OpenImages.
neurips-2021-large-scale-unsupervised-ob.tldr: LOD turns unsupervised object discovery into a ranking problem that scales to millions of images while improving reported discovery performance.

paragraphs: A system with several power-saving states must decide how deeply to sleep during an idle period whose duration is unknown. Different states consume different amounts of energy and impose different wake-up costs. The best decision therefore depends on future inactivity, making predictions potentially useful but also creating a need to handle prediction errors.

The paper develops an online algorithm that incorporates predicted idle durations without assuming they are accurate. Its performance is near optimal when predictions are accurate and worsens gracefully as prediction error grows. It also retains a worst-case guarantee almost matching that of the optimal classical online algorithm, connecting predictive benefits with protection against poor forecasts.

A key technical ingredient is a new learning-augmented algorithm for the ski-rental problem, with tight dependence on prediction error. The authors use this ingredient to address the multiple-state power-management setting and support the theoretical findings with experiments. The contribution is thus a quantified relationship between forecast quality and energy-management performance, rather than a requirement that forecasts always be dependable.
neurips-2021-learning-augmented-dynamic-.tldr: The proposed power-management algorithm benefits from accurate idle-time predictions while retaining strong worst-case protection when predictions are wrong.

paragraphs: Probability models can contain symmetries: transformations of a configuration that leave its density unchanged. This paper uses such structure to improve both sampling and learning. Its central idea is to incorporate symmetry into the procedure that generates samples, so the learning process can exploit information already present in the form of the target distribution.

The authors introduce Equivariant Stein Variational Gradient Descent, a sampling algorithm based on Stein’s identity. Equivariant kernels explicitly encode symmetry information in the sampler. The paper reports benefits in sample complexity and generated-sample quality, making symmetry part of the computational mechanism rather than merely a property of the distribution being modeled.

The authors then define equivariant energy-based models for invariant densities and train them through contrastive divergence using the proposed sampler. Combining the structured model with the structured sampling procedure offers ways to improve and scale energy-based training. Applications include joint-density modeling for image regression and classification, many-body particle systems, and molecular structure generation, illustrating the framework across several kinds of symmetric probabilistic problems.
neurips-2021-learning-equivariant-energy.tldr: The paper incorporates symmetry into Stein variational sampling and energy-based models to improve sampling and support more efficient training.

paragraphs: Algorithms can supply supervision beyond ordinary labels, including ordering requirements or image silhouettes. Integrating them into neural training is difficult when their discrete decisions interrupt smooth differentiation. This paper develops a general relaxation approach intended to make algorithmic components usable within end-to-end trainable networks, extending beyond relaxations designed around one particular task.

The method approximates discrete conditions inside conditional statements, loops, and indexing operations. It perturbs relevant variables using logistic distributions and approximates the expected result under those perturbations. The resulting computations become smoothly differentiable, providing gradients that can pass through algorithmic operations and guide the neural components connected to them.

This matters because the relaxation is organized around common programming structures rather than a single application’s custom formulation. The authors evaluate the approach on four challenging tasks and find that it can keep pace with task-specific relaxations. These results support the possibility of a more reusable route to algorithmic supervision while preserving competitive performance in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-learning-with-algorithmic-s.tldr: A general relaxation of discrete control structures makes algorithms differentiable and competitive with task-specific relaxations on four evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Vector autoregressive models describe how several time-varying quantities depend on earlier values through a transition matrix. Estimating that matrix becomes challenging in high dimensions, where structural restrictions help make the problem manageable. This paper studies how quickly gradient-based optimization can estimate such structured matrices from temporally dependent observations.

The authors analyze projected gradient descent for a matrix with a single structure and alternating projected gradient descent for a superposition of structures. They prove that both algorithms converge at a linear rate until reaching the statistical error level. Here, linear convergence describes geometric reduction of optimization error, while the statistical error marks the estimation accuracy supported by the data.

The guarantees hold despite the absence of strong convexity in the high-dimensional objective. They are non-asymptotic, addressing finite settings rather than only limiting behavior. The results also match the corresponding independent-sample model’s phase-transition theory up to a constant factor. Numerical experiments support the analysis, linking practical gradient methods to sharp optimization guarantees for structured time-series estimation.
neurips-2021-linear-convergence-of-gradi.tldr: The paper proves linear convergence to statistical accuracy for projected gradient methods estimating structured high-dimensional autoregressive models.

paragraphs: A GAN’s latent representation can contain directions that control meaningful image attributes, but discovered directions often change an image globally. LowRankGAN seeks more precise control by starting with a particular image region, such as the eyes in a face. It studies how changes in the latent code relate to changes in that region.

The method represents this relationship with a Jacobian matrix and applies low-rank factorization to identify steerable latent subspaces. The factorization also produces a null space: directions that leave the selected region unaffected while changing its surroundings. Projecting an attribute direction into this space enables region-selective editing without relying on a spatial mask.

The authors report that these low-dimensional representations make editing more precise and controllable. They also find that subspaces analyzed using a local region in one image generalize to other images, reducing the amount of analysis required for use. Experiments with StyleGAN2 and BigGAN trained on multiple datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness, supporting local sensitivity analysis as a practical route to finer control of generated images.
neurips-2021-low-rank-subspaces-in-gans-.tldr: LowRankGAN factors region-specific Jacobians to discover latent directions for more precise, transferable control of generated images.

paragraphs: Lidar measurements can become extremely sparse for small or distant objects, even when an onboard color camera shows those objects clearly. This paper addresses that mismatch by using camera information to enrich the input to a lidar-based 3D detector. The aim is to make useful visual evidence available in the detector’s existing point-based representation.

The method starts from 2D detections and generates dense virtual points in 3D. These points augment the original lidar cloud and enter the detector alongside actual lidar measurements. Representing the additional information as points allows the approach to integrate naturally with standard lidar-based detectors, rather than requiring a separate recognition output to be reconciled afterward.

On the nuScenes dataset, the resulting multimodal system improves a strong CenterPoint baseline by 6.6 mAP and outperforms competing fusion approaches. The finding supports virtual-point augmentation as a simple, effective way to combine complementary sensors. In particular, it shows that camera-derived information can improve 3D recognition through the same input format already used for sparse lidar observations.
neurips-2021-multimodal-virtual-point-3d.tldr: Camera-derived virtual 3D points enrich sparse lidar clouds, improving CenterPoint by 6.6 mAP on nuScenes.

paragraphs: Bootstrapping uses variations of the training data to produce multiple fitted models, supporting ensembles and uncertainty estimation. With deep networks, repeatedly resampling and training models can be expensive. Neural Bootstrapper addresses this bottleneck by learning to generate bootstrapped predictions through a single model-training process, making the uncertainty workflow less computationally demanding.

The method, called NeuBoots, injects bootstrap weights into high-level feature layers of a backbone network. Those weights let the model output bootstrapped target predictions without adding parameters or repeatedly recomputing training from scratch. The design moves the variation needed for bootstrap predictions into the network’s feature processing rather than requiring separately trained networks for each variation.

The authors apply NeuBoots to prediction calibration in image classification and semantic segmentation, active learning, and out-of-distribution detection. Their empirical results show better performance than other bagging-based methods at substantially lower computational cost, while preserving the validity of bootstrapping. These findings support the method as a way to make bootstrap-based uncertainty tools more practical across several learning tasks.
neurips-2021-neural-bootstrapper-6b7d656.tldr: NeuBoots generates bootstrap predictions from one trained network, reducing computation while supporting effective uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: Automatic dubbing must do more than read a script clearly: the generated speech must fit the timing of an existing video. Neural Dubber frames this as a multimodal text-to-speech task, combining the words to be spoken with visual evidence about how the speaker is moving. This brings synchronization into the speech-generation process itself.

The model uses lip movements to control speech prosody, connecting the delivery of the script to the recorded video. For videos containing different speakers, an image-based speaker embedding module uses the speaker’s face to generate a reasonable vocal timbre. The stated aim is a suitable voice characteristic, rather than a claim of recovering the speaker’s exact voice.

Experiments use a single-speaker chemistry lecture dataset and the multi-speaker LRS2 dataset. Reported speech quality is on par with state-of-the-art text-to-speech systems. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations also show video-guided prosody and high-fidelity speech synchronized with the footage. Together, these findings support generating convincing audio while using visual timing to meet the additional requirements of dubbing.
neurips-2021-neural-dubber-dubbing-for-v.tldr: Neural Dubber uses scripts and visible lip movements to generate high-quality speech synchronized with video.

paragraphs: Learning Hamiltonian dynamics often assumes that observations already use generalized positions and momenta. In real data, the necessary momenta may be unknown, making that representation difficult to obtain. This paper learns the geometric structure underlying Hamiltonian equations so that training data can remain in more general coordinate systems.

The approach uses a coordinate-free description based on a symplectic two-form. Rather than directly learning an arbitrary skew-symmetric matrix, which need not define a valid symplectic form, the model learns a differential one-form with a neural network and derives the two-form through an exterior derivative. The authors use this construction to improve learning efficiency.

The resulting method can model equations expressed through either Hamiltonian or Lagrangian formalisms and extract hidden Hamiltonian structure from data. Numerical experiments show recovery of nontrivial structures in polynomial ordinary differential equations, including the Lotka-Volterra equation. The contribution is a route to learning structured dynamics when the convenient canonical coordinates are not already supplied, with experimental evidence that concealed structure can be recovered.
neurips-2021-neural-symplectic-form-lear.tldr: Learning a symplectic form lets neural models recover Hamiltonian dynamics from data expressed in general coordinate systems.

paragraphs: Lévy flights are random walks that combine many short movements with occasional large jumps through a heavy-tailed step-size distribution. Such patterns appear in animal search and human cognition, but their circuit-level origin remains unresolved. This paper investigates whether noisy adaptation within attractor neural networks can generate this kind of movement in the network’s internal state.

The authors first study continuous attractor networks with spike-frequency adaptation. Adaptation strength defines a boundary between local Brownian movement and long-jump movement. Noise in adaptation causes intermittent switching between these modes, producing Lévy-flight characteristics. The proposed mechanism therefore links a particular source of neural variability to the mixture of movement scales.

The study then extends the mechanism to a more general attractor network. The authors demonstrate that their model can explain Lévy-flight patterns observed during human free memory retrieval. This offers a possible neural account of those observations and connects circuit dynamics to cognitive search behavior. It does not establish that noisy adaptation is the unique mechanism underlying all Lévy-flight phenomena.
neurips-2021-noisy-adaptation-generates-.tldr: Noisy neural adaptation can generate Lévy-flight-like state transitions by switching attractor networks between local motion and long jumps.

paragraphs: Chip design requires placing components and routing the connections between them. Machine learning offers GPU acceleration and reduced reliance on expert decisions, but connecting these tasks within an effective learning process remains challenging. This paper develops joint learning methods to coordinate placement decisions and better connect placement with the routing stage that follows.

For macros and standard cells, the authors combine reinforcement learning with gradient-based optimization. They also develop a reinforcement-learning approach linking placement to routing. A multi-view embedding represents both the global graph of input macros and information about individual nodes, giving the learning system access to the overall design and its local components.

Random network distillation encourages exploration within this learning process. Experiments on public chip-design benchmarks show that the method learns from experience and produces high-quality intermediate placements for subsequent standard-cell placement, with training taking a few hours. The stated outcome supports useful coordination within the design flow, particularly through the quality of intermediate placements supplied to later processing.
neurips-2021-on-joint-learning-for-solvi.tldr: Joint reinforcement learning and gradient optimization coordinate chip placement and routing, producing useful intermediate placements after a few hours of training.

paragraphs: This paper connects two views of a neural network: how its loss changes when parameters move and how its output changes when inputs move. The link comes from the multiplicative interaction between input data and first-layer parameters. Using this relationship, the authors show how flat minima constrain the model’s input gradient, offering an explanation for their generalization behavior.

The analysis then extends beyond flatness to higher-order moments of gradient noise. By examining the linear stability of stochastic gradient descent around global minima, the authors show that SGD tends to constrain these moments. Combining this with the first-layer relationship translates properties of the optimization process into restrictions on the learned function.

The resulting effect is described as Sobolev regularization: SGD controls derivative-based measures of the model function with respect to its inputs. The paper also derives bounds on generalization error and adversarial robustness under assumptions about the data distribution. These conditional guarantees connect training stability with input smoothness, while keeping the conclusions tied to the setting of the analysis.
neurips-2021-on-linear-stability-of-sgd-.tldr: The paper links SGD stability to input smoothness and derives conditional generalization and adversarial-robustness bounds.

paragraphs: One way to understand a recurrent neural network is to approximate its dynamics near fixed points with linear systems. Choosing the relevant fixed point can be difficult, and approximation errors can accumulate. This paper addresses both problems by co-training an RNN with a switching linear dynamical system designed to track its behavior.

The linear system uses first-order Taylor expansions of the RNN and an auxiliary function that selects fixed points throughout state space. Joint training produces a close approximation and regularizes the RNN so that first-order terms perform the computation when possible. This removes the separate post-training fixed-point optimization and provides an unambiguous linear-system description at each state.

The formulation also supports continuous manifolds of switching points while sharing parameters across switches. The authors validate its usefulness on two synthetic tasks connected to earlier RNN interpretation work. They then incorporate it into LFADS and analyze single-trial spiking activity from a non-human primate’s motor system, demonstrating how the interpretable dynamical component can participate in a more complex modeling architecture.
neurips-2021-reverse-engineering-recurre.tldr: Co-training an RNN with a switching linear model makes its dynamics easier to interpret while maintaining a close approximation.

paragraphs: A simple representation of optimal action values does not automatically make reinforcement learning sample efficient. This paper studies settings where the optimal Q-function is linear in given features. Even with a large gap between optimal and suboptimal choices, feasibility depends on how the learner is allowed to obtain observations.

The authors introduce a sampling protocol that explores online but permits backtracking to previously visited states. It sits between standard online interaction and access to a generative model: the learner can revisit its experience, but it does not receive the broader sampling freedom of the latter. This change creates a distinct setting for investigating linear value representations.

An algorithm tailored to this protocol has sample complexity polynomial in feature dimension, horizon, and the inverse suboptimality gap, without depending on the size of the state or action space. The result shows that limited revisiting can enable sample-efficient learning under the stated representation and gap conditions. Its significance lies in the interaction between representation simplicity and data access, rather than linear realizability alone.
neurips-2021-sample-efficient-reinforcem.tldr: Allowing limited revisits enables sample-efficient reinforcement learning with linear optimal action values under the stated gap conditions.

paragraphs: Contrastive pretraining often benefits from large collections of unlabeled images, but obtaining even unlabeled medical scans can be difficult and costly. This paper studies segmentation when no additional unlabeled data is available. It instead uses meta-labels already associated with acquisition, such as a two-dimensional slice’s location within a three-dimensional MRI scan.

These weak annotations guide both encoder pretraining and a semi-supervised learning stage using a reduced set of detailed annotations. A self-paced strategy further uses the meta-labels to distinguish useful supervision from noise. The approach therefore extracts training information from the available scans and their acquisition context, reducing reliance on either extra scans or extensive segmentation labels.

Across five medical segmentation datasets, the method substantially improves a model trained on only a few scans and outperforms previous contrastive and semi-supervised approaches. It also approaches the performance of a model trained on the full data. These empirical results suggest that acquisition metadata can provide valuable supervision when both scan availability and detailed annotation are constrained.
neurips-2021-self-paced-contrastive-lear.tldr: Acquisition meta-labels and self-paced contrastive learning improve medical segmentation with few annotated scans and no additional unlabeled data.

paragraphs: Steerable convolutions learn 3D features that transform consistently when objects rotate or translate. Their computational cost on dense volumes can make them poorly suited to inherently sparse 3D data. This paper introduces Sparse Steerable Convolution, or SS-Conv, to accelerate this processing while strictly retaining SE(3)-equivariance, the required consistency under rigid spatial transformations.

SS-Conv operates with sparse tensors and serves as the foundation for an object-pose estimation pipeline. A Feature-Steering module exploits the equivariant features to refine pose efficiently. The contribution connects the mathematical transformation property with a practical refinement operation, making that property useful throughout the estimation process rather than only in feature extraction.

Experiments cover instance-level pose estimation, category-level pose and size estimation, and category-level pose tracking. The pipeline outperforms existing methods on almost all evaluated metrics across these tasks. Ablation studies also favor SS-Conv over alternative convolutions in both accuracy and efficiency. These findings support sparse computation as a way to make equivariant 3D processing more practical without surrendering its defining transformation behavior.
neurips-2021-sparse-steerable-convolutio.tldr: SS-Conv accelerates equivariant 3D feature learning on sparse data and supports accurate, efficient object-pose estimation and tracking.
